details:
VitalOrbit is a static web dashboard (HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Chart.js vendored so it works fully offline) that helps an astronaut assess their own health during a mission. The crew overview shows four fictional demo astronauts with an overall green, amber or red status. Selecting a crew member opens their vitals panel: heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO2), sleep, stress and mood score, exercise minutes and radiation dose, each shown with its current value, its safe-range band and its status, updating every few seconds from a clearly labelled simulated feed. Seven-day trend charts for heart rate, SpO2, sleep and radiation dose show the safe range as a green band, so a slow drift is visible before it becomes an emergency. A rule-based alert engine evaluates thresholds on every reading — for example, resting heart rate above 100 bpm for consecutive readings raises an amber alert — and every alert carries a plain-language recommended action such as "Rest, hydrate, re-check in 30 min". An environment switcher (Spacecraft, ISS, Moon, Mars) changes the hazard context, radiation dose rates and countermeasures shown. A dedicated 5-Hazards view maps each of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight to the vitals it affects, its current risk level and the countermeasure being tracked. A daily health timeline schedules exercise, meals, sleep and check-ins and flags overdue items, and a rule-based health chatbot answers about fifteen common questions with a short education note under each answer. The benefit is speed and clarity for the person who has to act: on a long mission the astronaut is the first responder, and a colour-first screen with a concrete action beats a table of numbers — especially with Earth minutes away by radio. For mission control the same screen covers the whole crew at once. The intended impact is earlier action: problems are caught while they are still trends, not emergencies. VitalOrbit is creative in that it is built for the astronaut, not the doctor: colour-first status, plain-language actions, reminders and a teaching chatbot, all organised around the five-hazards framework rather than around a single vital sign. We considered the factors NASA lists for this challenge: different environments (spacecraft, ISS, Moon, Mars), prompts and reminders to act, dynamic charts over time, colour coding readable at a glance, and educational material through the chatbot. The risk model and thresholds are grounded in NASA Human Research Program material — the 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight, Risks of Human Spaceflight and Ongoing HRP Research pages, plus Canadian Space Agency material on monitoring radiation for astronaut health — and in open HRP data portals (NASA Open Science Data Repository and NASA Life Sciences Portal) used for background reference ranges. Reference ranges used: resting heart rate 60–100 bpm, SpO2 95–100%, sleep 7–9 hours, exercise 120 minutes per day (ISS countermeasure protocol), ISS dose of 0.40 mSv per day as a simulation assumption (600 mSv career limit, NASA-STD-3001). All live values are simulated demo data for fictional crew members, labelled as such throughout the app; VitalOrbit is a monitoring and awareness tool, not a medical device and not a diagnosis. No NASA logos, branding, flags or mission identifiers are used anywhere. Code and demo deck: https://github.com/iamartya15/vitalorbit-space-apps-2026

Since the first draft, VitalOrbit gained four capabilities. A Scenario Simulator in the header offers three what-if controls: Nominal Orbit, Solar Particle Event and CO2 Scrubber Drift. A solar particle event multiplies the radiation dose rate and fires a shielded-module alert; a CO2 scrubber drift makes crew SpO2 fall and resting heart rate rise across the crew while firing a scrubber alert with a concrete recovery action; returning to Nominal restores baseline values. The alert engine now includes a composite risk rule: when short sleep (under 6 h), high stress (above 7/10) and elevated resting heart rate (above 100 bpm) coincide in one astronaut, it raises a single high-priority Compound Fatigue & Cardiovascular Strain alert, because the combination multiplies fatigue and cardiac strain beyond any single reading. The health chatbot is now context-aware: questions about your own state (How am I doing? Is my heart rate normal?) are answered from the selected crew member's current live values with range comparisons and advice, while general questions still use the rule-based Q&A bank. Radiation dose is tracked per crew member rather than per spacecraft: each astronaut carries an exposure factor for EVA work and time in shielded modules, so daily doses differ across the crew, and switching environment rescales the 7-day radiation history to the new dose rate instead of showing a false spike.
